content.rationale: The requirement sentences with a runnable artifact dependent: conformance is what running the artifact shows, so the gate states the observables the sentences demand and leaves the verdict to the run. The check draws the graph where the surface draws it (rtlotqvy): a node's element is placed at its layout box less the layout's bounds origin, and the drawn graph spans from the surface origin to the layout's bounds size, so a drawn box is not a layout box except where that origin is (0,0). Every page the geometry clauses run on is prepared so that origin is not (0,0) on either axis — the graph is laid out, one of its boxes is dragged past the layout's own left edge, and an unresolved edge stands above the first row — and the check asserts the origin it is left on before reading anything, so a reading of the layout's own coordinates where the surface draws drawn ones is off by the origin at every geometric assertion instead of passing on a page whose origin happened to be (0,0) on an axis. The geometry clauses therefore read the box the surface draws for a node, the extent the surface draws for the graph, and the layout point the surface draws under the pointer, and take the fitted and overflowing axes, the pan rests and the centring expectations from those drawn readings rather than from the layout's own coordinates, on a graph fitted to each panel size driven here, a graph zoomed out until it fits, and the pan and zoom the viewer starts from with one axis overflowing. The interaction must also apply each state change incrementally per stppxysx — a selection, hover, drag or keyboard focus change looks up the elements the change affects by the identity it carries and writes only those, and the changes pending within a frame are merged into at most one application to the surface, carrying the last pending value rather than dropping it. The check draws its own surface from the layout the interaction asks its delegate for, using only the page interface's identity attributes and the layout module (ympqvvwr, qmsmvrnr), so it runs at this node's base with no renderer in the graph; the real-renderer integration stays with ylolxwpv. It drives real pointer and key events and observes, per change, every element lookup the interaction makes on the surface or on anything the surface contains — any of querySelector, querySelectorAll, getElementsByClassName and getElementsByTagName, with any selector, so naming no selector cannot hide the read — together with the class writes it asks of each drawn element and the relayout calls it makes for one drag within a frame. The check also drives pointer gestures the way a browser delivers them: a press lands on the element under the pointer, the release and the rest of that gesture are addressed where the surface's document was asked to send them (pointer capture when the gesture takes it, the element under the pointer otherwise), and the compatibility event a repeated press produces is addressed to the nearest common inclusive ancestor of the two clicks' targets. The check therefore also spans a graph reload (uvmutyww): the renderer draws the new revision in elements of its own and the page hands the interaction the new graph through the page interface's graph swap, so the two clicks of one double click no longer share the pressed element and the compatibility event lands on the surface whoever is capturing — an addressing the gesture's own capture choice cannot move back onto the pressed node, which is why the check cannot be satisfied by fulfilling the requirement through keeping the browser's addressing where it started. Read back through the delegate's request to open a node's document and through the selection it reports, the check observes that a gesture acts on the subject its press landed on — a node, an edge or the empty canvas — unchanged for the whole gesture, and that each gesture's subject is its own. The check also spans the focus that recentres the viewport (wzsxvmvw): a focus arriving at a node by a means other than a pointer click on that node — keyboard traversal forwards and backwards, and the interaction's own focus move — is observed to leave the viewport on the box the surface draws for that node, with the zoom level unchanged. What the move must leave is taken per axis from the rule and from the extent the layout module draws, never from the limits the behaviour keeps, because the rule draws the line per axis: on an axis where the drawn graph fits within the viewport at the zoom in hand — observed after the viewer frames the graph, after the panel is resized to each size the check drives, and after the graph is zoomed out until it fits — the node's centre is observed at the centre of the canvas exactly, with the margin the rule permits at the graph's edge, and the expectation is not clamped by any limit the behaviour enforces; on an axis where the drawn graph overflows the viewport — observed beside a fitted axis, at the pan and zoom the viewer starts from — the graph is observed to keep covering the viewport, the pan limits read back from the behaviour by panning to each side at the zoom in hand are observed to bind the move, and the check records that accepted boundary: the view comes to rest on a recorded limit and no further there, and the node is not observed centred on that axis. The limit a pan itself keeps is observed where the drawn extent and the canvas's own size put it rather than read back from the behaviour (yymrxqsk), because a limit read back by panning follows a changed clamp instead of naming it: on an axis the drawn graph fits at the zoom in hand — the graph framed to each of the sizes the panel is resized to, and the graph zoomed out until it fits — a pan driven far to each side is observed to leave the viewport at that one place, with the graph's near edge on the canvas's near edge at one extreme and its far edge on the canvas's far edge at the other, and on an axis the graph overflows the view is observed to come to rest with the graph covering the canvas, its far edge on the canvas's far edge at one extreme and its near edge on the canvas's near edge at the other. The boundary of the two readings is driven too: an axis whose drawn extent is exactly the canvas's own is observed to be the fitted one, so a pan holds that axis at the single place it allows and a focus move onto a node still brings the node's centre to the centre of the canvas there — which an axis treated as overflowing on equality fails. The means the recentre must not reach are driven the same way: a pointer click on a node (still selecting it and reporting the selection, ltrnmrsr), a change of the panel's own focus (pltovtuo), and a focus that ends with no node focused as when a reload re-reads the documents without the focused node — each is observed to leave the viewport exactly as it was. A recentre is also observed to be a viewport move and nothing else: the traversal order and its wrap, the focus emphasis on the focused node (ozxnxzus), the zoom level and the selection a click produced stay as their own decisions set them. It is observed against the bound the interaction already carries (mntwwzyl, stppxysx) with a selection dimming and brightening the drawn elements in place: the focus move that recentres makes no element lookup on the surface, writes no class to any drawn element but the one the focus emphasis moves to, moves no drawn box, and leaves the surface the single transform a pan to the same viewport writes, read back from a surface panned there at the same zoom rather than restated. The same rule reaches a node the interaction is asked about rather than one focus lands on: the page declares its request to bring a named node into view (ympqvvwr), and the interaction must answer that request with that very centring move rather than with a second one beside it. The request is driven on the same graphs, at the same zooms and on the same canvas sizes as the focus clause, and its expectation is read the same way, off the layout the interaction asks its delegate for and the canvas's own size rather than off any limit the behaviour keeps: a fitted axis takes the named node's centre to the centre of the canvas with the margin the rule permits and no recorded limit applied, an overflowing axis keeps the graph covering the viewport with the recorded pan limit binding so the move comes to rest on that limit and the node is not centred there, and an axis the graph fills exactly counts as fitted whichever of the two the check drives. Because the reuse is observed as the move's outcome and not as the shape of the code, the check drives the request and the focus arrival on separate surfaces prepared alike — same graph, same zoom, same canvas — and compares the viewport each comes to rest on and the surface transform each writes; it cannot tell one shared move from a second move written apart that agrees at every state driven here, and it does not try to, but a second move that diverges anywhere is visible: another node centred, a clamp re-derived instead of the rule's per-axis reading, an axis treated as overflowing on its equality boundary, or a transform written apart from the one path a pan takes. The request is also held to being a viewport move and nothing else, in the window one change opens: it reads no part of the surface, writes no class to any drawn element — the focus emphasis included, since a request to show where a node is is not a focus move and does not move the node focus — moves no drawn box, re-lays nothing out, opens no document and changes neither the selection nor the selection it reports, while the view does move, so the clause is about a centring move and not about a request that did nothing. The request is called by the name the interface declares it under, taken from the interface the interaction implements (ympqvvwr) rather than spelled as this check's own, and a controller that does not answer it at all stops the check at that point naming the request. Nothing here fixes the name of any private function, an amount scrolled, an animation or a smoothness of the move: what the request leaves and what it writes are observed, not how it gets there.
